items.title: You’re allowed to be happy. In fact, you have a duty to be.
items.summary: Albert Camus and Simone de Beauvoir were having a drink when de Beauvoir asked how anybody can be happy in a world so full of misery. How can they laugh and drink and dance when millions of people are being murdered and abused? It’s a good question, and one I’m sure many of us have asked at one time or another. Unless you’ve made a deliberate effort to avoid even a glimpse of the news, you know that the world contains vast and intense suffering: wars, murders, and abuse, of course, but also sickness, famine, and natural disaster. How is it ever okay to clink glasses of champagne while children are dying? How can we so easily sleep at night knowing that someone, somewhere, is being tortured? And then Camus gave his answer: “Happiness exists, and it’s important; why refuse it?” Camus argued that refusing joy does nothing to cure the misery in the world. It merely adds your misery to the total sum. It makes us less capable of defeating it. A Brief for the Defense In 2005, the poet Jack Gilbert published a poem called “A Brief for the Defense,” where he imagined a defendant accused of having joy. The world contains famine and torture and children dying in places you will never see. And so how can you dare to laugh? How can you be happy while others are suffering? Gilbert’s answer, like Camus’s, is to say that if suffering exists and you respond by extinguishing your own joy, then suffering has produced two losses rather than one. First, there is the pain itself: the bullet, the scream, the anguish. And then, there is the echo — the suffering that comes from focusing too long on the suffering. We shouldn’t allow misery to win twice. In fact, he even goes further than this, further than most people are comfortable with. Gilbert says delight isn’t only permitted, but that you have a duty to feel delight. To deny yourself joy when the world contains so much horror would allow horror to set the terms. When so much of the world is dark, we are responsible all the more for bringing in some light. Gilbert and Camus were not saying that we should ignore suffering, or that we shouldn’t try to help. Rather, they were saying that our pain doesn’t relieve the world’s pain. In fact, Camus argued the opposite: Accepting happiness makes us better equipped to fight for it. For our tomorrow In 1946, among the ruins of Nazi Germany, the philosopher Karl Jaspers described something similar to de Beauvoir’s unease but on a grander scale: what he called “metaphysical guilt.” This is not the guilt of anything you did, but it’s the guilt of simply surviving when others have not. It’s that unbearable guilt of being here when others could not be. It’s the happiness you enjoy that others cannot. Jaspers argued we cannot will this feeling away, but we can learn from it. We can learn that we are bound to all humans who have ever existed and will ever exist. When we adopt this metaphysical view, we see ourselves in solidarity with the species. History is a network, and our lives are webbed together. In my living, I represent life. I am writing this article in November, when many countries around the world mark a remembrance for those who died in conflict. And, in the UK at least, there’s a line that’s used a lot. It’s from the war memorial at Kohima: “For your tomorrow, we gave our today.” So, use it. Use the today that we have been gifted. Find all the joy that those who gave their lives could not. Camus, Gilbert, and Jaspers are getting at a similar thing. Pausing to appreciate the sacrifices of the past and present is important and respectful. Working as much as is reasonable to alleviate suffering is moral. But living as fully and happily as we can is a kind of duty. We should laugh loudly for those who cannot. We should enjoy the world’s wonders because so many are deprived of access to them. We should squeeze as much goodness from life as possible because that isn’t possible for millions. As the activist Dan Savage put it, “During the darkest days of the AIDS crisis, we buried our friends in the morning, we protested in the afternoon, and we danced all night. The dance kept us in the fight because it was the dance we were fighting for.” This article You’re allowed to be happy. In fact, you have a duty to be. is featured on Big Think .

items.title: The Worst Thing About AI Writing
items.summary: In 1968, Yambo Ouologuem was the toast of Paris. His first novel, Le devoir de violence , which traces the rise and fall of an African dynasty across centuries, was a best seller and won the Prix Renaudot, France’s second-most-prestigious literary prize. Ouologuem was the first African writer to receive the honor. The book continued to be celebrated until 1972, when the Times Literary Supplement published an extract of Le devoir de violence —in English, “Bound to Violence”—alongside a remarkably similar passage from Graham Greene ’s 1934 novel, It’s a Battlefield . Given that certain scene descriptions and dialogue appeared nearly word-for-word in each novel, Ouologuem’s astonishing debut seemed at least partially plagiarized. The story quickly became global news. Ouologuem’s American publisher pulped thousands of copies of the novel’s English translation. The head of Le Seuil, Ouologuem’s French publisher, called the accusations of plagiarism “exaggerated,” but Ouologuem accused Le Seuil of launching a smear-filled “press campaign” to avoid paying royalties. Communications with his publisher soon ceased, and Ouologuem returned to his native Mali. He continued to write privately, his son later said, but he never published again. This past September, a Haitian Canadian author named Thélyson Orélien came to Paris as the toast of what the French call the rentrée littéraire , or “fall publishing season.” Orélien, who had been on the margins of the literary scene in Quebec, had quickly become a star in France, and he was now living what one critic called a “ conte de fées ”—a “fairy tale.” C’était ça ou mourir —in English, “It Was Either That or Die”—is the story of a Haitian schoolteacher who, driven from his native country by gang violence, attempts to make his way north to Canada, a journey that is often dangerous and degrading. It’s much less stylish and thought-provoking than Bound to Violence , but it became a best seller in France; won the Prix du Roman Fnac, the first major award of the rentrée ; and was in the running for the Renaudot and the even more prestigious Prix Goncourt. Then, on September 21—the same day that Orélien won the Fnac—a small, anonymous account on X posted an analysis of several chapters of the novel by the AI-detection tool Pangram, which claimed that 100 percent of the text analyzed was written by AI. Soon afterward, the newsmagazine Le Point reported on several instances of alleged plagiarism in Orélien’s early work, which the author later admitted to and apologized for. The Académie Goncourt disqualified him. Late last month, the Quebecois publisher of Orélien’s book announced that he had in fact used AI, despite his denials, and ended their relationship; his French publisher, Éditions Grasset, continues to sell the book. (Orélien, who in one of his latest public statements called the attacks he was experiencing a “media lynching,” did not respond to multiple requests for comment via e-mail and through his publishers.) [ Read: Yet another literary prizewinner seems to be AI ] The scandal was a reminder of how much—and how little—has changed in the French literary world since the uproar over Ouologuem’s work more than five decades ago. Although some of Orélien’s detractors voiced an earnest interest in authorial integrity, anyone following the online backlash against him could see that some of it was tinged with racism. Several commentators, for example, attacked Orélien’s command of the French language, suggesting that he lacked the ability to write his own work—a malevolent criticism that has long been marshaled against Black writers in France, including Ouologuem. And some of Orélien’s supporters, like Ouologuem’s, seemed determined to overlook the serious evidence against him out of loyalty to the narrative that he advanced. Above the chaos is a question: Why did this novel, thematically rote and stylistically bland as it is, receive such acclaim in the first place? S amuel Fitoussi , a young columnist for Le Figaro who is known for satirical columns that often target progressive ideals, is a member of the group behind Balance ton Claude, the X account that first alleged that Orélien had used AI. Its first posts argue that some influencers on X, including on the political right, were using AI without disclosing it. Fitoussi, who also works at a venture-capital firm that has invested in AI, looked into Orélien’s novel after a friend read it and suspected AI use. When we met in Paris in October, Fitoussi told me that he saw sharing Balance ton Claude’s findings as a matter of fairness. He worries that writers who “finish second in those prizes will not get noticed,” making victory by an AI-aided text more troubling and “discouraging humans to write.” But Fitoussi didn’t think that Orélien should be condemned wholesale over his apparent AI use. In a post for the Substack Persuasion, the Balance ton Claude collective wrote, “What matters here isn’t Orélien’s race or nationality, or our political views (or the political views that are sometimes attributed to us)” but rather “whether we are willing to have our literary and public discourse overwhelmed by AI writing—and whether we really will deprive ourselves of the discernment to tell the difference.” [ Read: The human skill that eludes AI ] That effort to depoliticize the incident came too late: Commentators on both the left and the right had already retreated to their respective corners. The left seized on the fact that allegations of AI use in fiction have focused disproportionately on Black writers, critiqued Fitoussi’s personal politics, and claimed that AI-detection technology is not reliable. (Although Pangram remains susceptible to false negatives—meaning that it can incorrectly flag AI writing as human— some research suggests that its rate of false positives is very low.) Meanwhile, the right harped on the hollowness of literary institutions that it claimed were more interested in ideology than in literature. In Valeurs Actuelles , a far-right magazine, the critic Alix Avril argued that the novel’s subject matter had made it verboten to critique on literary grounds. “The hero is a migrant,” she wrote. “Consequently, the book is irreproachable. To criticize it is to risk being relegated to the camp of the salauds ”—an insult that roughly translates to “assholes.” At the same time, a third camp warned against judging the political value of the novel by how it was allegedly written. The 2021 Prix Goncourt winner, Mohamed Mbougar Sarr, writing in French, argued that someone testing immigrant writers with an AI detector doesn’t automatically make them a xenophobe, but also noted that stories about immigration are “the obsession of the fachosphère ”—a term for the nationalist far right. It would be a mistake to discount the novel’s humanity, he added, just because the text appeared to have been generated by machines. “I did not say to myself, after finishing it, that it was an AI-generated book,” Sarr wrote. “I attributed its weaknesses to the limits and clumsiness of the writer.” The narrator of C’était ça ou mourir , 29-year-old Jonas Dorléon, is portrayed as being something close to an angel in disguise. He manages to survive an extraordinarily hostile migrant’s journey without once taking advantage of someone else, or even considering the possibility of doing so. His fellow migrants are docile and possessed of Job-like patience. No one complains or raises their voice. Individually almost indistinguishable, they appear to exist merely to deliver proverbs in portentous tones. “Do you know why I would like to die before you?” a Peruvian migrant asks Jonas. “Because if I die before, at least you could tell the tale.” Afterward, the narrator uses a “not X, but Y” formulation that is typical of AI writing, and that appears dozens of times throughout the book. “He did not say this emphatically,” Jonas says, “not like a phrase destined to leave a mark. items.title: A Novel About Obsessively Digging Into the Past
items.summary: Reconstructing the past is, depending on whom you ask, a fool’s errand, a great hobby, or a vital source of knowledge and meaning. Many families have a de facto genealogist: a cousin or an uncle who loves Ancestry.com, spends hours digging for long-lost relatives, or organizes trips to their forebears’ hometowns. My husband’s grandfather, whose own grandfather immigrated to the United States from Scotland, felt so connected to that heritage that he attended reunions of their Scottish clan. But for many, the desire to touch the past goes far beyond ancestry. If it didn’t, no one would travel to the sites of old battles or participate, unpaid, in historical reenactments—popular activities that suggest a wish to identify with bigger forms of history. Especially for people who can’t trace their family tree very far, reaching for a national or cultural past can be a way to feel grounded in their present self. What Remains , an excellent debut novel by the Galician writer Brais Lamela, follows its unnamed narrator as he engages in one such quest. A graduate student, he gets sidetracked from his dissertation by his ever more obsessive drive to fully recreate life in the precise time and place he studies. It’s no coincidence that the place in question is the exact part of Galicia, a mountainous, mostly coastal region in northwestern Spain, where he grew up. The narrator now lives in New York, and over the course of the novel, Lamela makes clear that his protagonist’s determination to reconstruct the past soothes his sense that he’s untethered and alone in his adopted country. Lamela, like his protagonist, is based in New York. He wrote What Remains in Galician, which is not spoken in most of Spain and isn’t a common literary language; his translator, Jacob Rogers, has noted that it’s “on the margins of the Spanish market.” For Lamela to write in Galician rather than Spanish, then, is an artistic expression of commitment to his particular roots. So is the subject of his narrator’s research—which is, inevitably, one of the main subjects of the novel itself. In the 1950s, Francisco Franco, the right-wing dictator who ruled Spain from the end of its civil war until his death, in 1975, decided that Galicia’s rural peasants needed to be modernized. To do this, his regime built dams that submerged much of Negueira de Muñiz, an especially remote, alpine part of the region. The government then demanded that the drowned villages’ inhabitants migrate to a lowland area called the Terra Chá. As Lamela writes in a foreword, the dictatorship designed this colonization plan to “break the habits of these peasants, whom they saw as backward and poor, and turn them into modern cattle ranchers.” The narrator is something of a dreamer who cannot research these events with the cool detachment that his thesis adviser recommends. Instead, he revels in an effort to recreate what’s gone. He imagines the peasants’ lives in vivid detail, straying from the evidence to conjure them listening to clandestine radio broadcasts in their bathrooms or yearning for the “particular shades of green or gray” that had characterized the now-flooded landscape of their home. Before long, the narrator gets fully sucked into a perhaps-quixotic effort to learn about one of these people, a widow named Leonita who resisted the regime’s control. His irritated adviser asks, not comprehending, “Why would you want to focus on a single life?” To the narrator, the reason is clear: When he reads about Leonita, he can feel what it might have been like to get dropped, against your will, into a new home. [ Read: The book that plunges you into messy American history ] Granted, the narrator isn’t a stranger to rootlessness. He emigrated voluntarily but still struggles with the “weightless and precarious” nature of living, without much money, far from home. As he gets ready to move in with his girlfriend, he reflects on how little he’s invested in the apartment he’s lived in for years. “I picked furniture that was easy to put together and take apart,” he notes, “as though I expected to leave at any moment.” Even after the move, the narrator seems most able to ground himself in his new home by wondering, “What would a group of archaeologists see if they happened upon the scene and tried to reconstruct our lives?” It is as if he can understand the world only through reconstruction, as if the process of recreation is, for him, a source of stability as much as it is an escape. Lamela’s narrator might be an extreme case—the main characters of novels tend to be—but he’s hardly alone in seeking both solace and meaning in the past. If he were, historical fiction would be far less popular among readers and writers alike; Americans wouldn’t travel to the Alamo or Colonial Williamsburg, let alone their ancestors’ faraway homes . In the 2024 movie A Real Pain , cousins played by Jesse Eisenberg and Kieran Culkin visit the house in Poland where their deceased grandmother lived before the Holocaust. It’s not easy to get there, and the experience is anticlimactic at best—they try to leave stones outside as remembrances, something Jews traditionally do at graves, and the house’s residents immediately point out that they’re a tripping hazard—yet the film never doubts that the cousins’ attempt to touch their grandmother’s pre–World War II life will connect them more closely to their shared history. In his 1998 book, Confederates in the Attic , the journalist Tony Horwitz joins a devoted Civil War reenactor named Robert Lee Hodge on an extreme quest to touch the past. Hodge takes a yearly trip, called the “Civil Wargasm,” that entails a week-long “high-speed trek from Gettysburg to Antietam to the Shenandoah Valley and dozens of battlefields in between,” dressed in the same reproduction-19th-century uniform and eating 19th-century rations the whole time. For Hodge, who at the time of Horwitz’s writing took a version of this journey once a year, the trip’s discomforts are a way to share what actual Civil War soldiers experienced. “This,” he tells Horwitz, “is the real deal.” It isn’t, of course. Nobody can get the past back, no matter how scratchy and unwashed the uniform they’re wearing is. What Hodge’s march gives him is a chance to make his imagination tangible. He’s still playing Civil War, and Horwitz makes clear that Hodge knows it. Yet the reenactor is compelled enough by the meaning that he derives from this connection to the past to want to maximize it—hardtack, chewing tobacco, and all. The physical discomfort that Hodge experiences during reenactments , however, doesn’t seem to extend to the moral realm. Over the course of Confederates in the Attic , it becomes clear that his minute attention to the details of the past allows him to avoid the big picture: When you’re imagining the individual hardships that one Confederate soldier endured, it’s easier to ignore the societal horror that he defended. Presumably for this reason, the reenactments Horwitz attends are all, as he writes, “blindingly white affairs.” Most of the reenactors Horwitz meets are also somewhat blithe about Civil War deaths. Only once does Horwitz meet somebody, a nurse who plays a grieving Union widow, who treats her hobby less as a vacation from the present than as an acknowledgment of past loss. “Glory had a cost,” she tells Horwitz. “I’m here so people will remember that.” She seems to share a hope with the narrator of What Remains ; both of them aspire to inhabit history so fully that they might create a home, or at least a moment of rest and acknowledgment, for its unsettled ghosts. [ Read: The cure for guilty memories ] Lamela’s narrator clearly also wants his dissertation, especially his Leonita research, to create a home of some sort for the unsettled parts of himself. In that sense, he has something in common with Hodge. Both want to ground themselves in essentially fictional connections—or at the very least, ones that can’t be reciprocated—to other

items.title: Now What?: How the Midterm Results Will Change America
items.summary: Republicans have suffered one of the worst midterm defeats in modern history. As they regroup, and Democrats weigh what to do with their new power, New Yorker writers asked people across the political spectrum—from Pete Buttigieg and Zohran Mamdani to Sarah Longwell and Oren Cass—what comes next.
items.title_original: Now What?: How the Midterm Results Will Change America
items.title_en: Now What?: How the Midterm Results Will Change America

items.title: AI proved a major quantum complexity conjecture. What does it mean?
items.summary: If you work with a normal computer — a classical computer — you’re used to two foundational ideas: the idea of bits, where information gets encoded as a “0” or “1” within some sort of storage medium or mechanism, and the idea of operations that can be performed on those bits (or “gates” that those bits can be passed through), which represent the possible computations that can be conducted with those bits. Some problems can be solved very efficiently with classical bits and classical gates, like four-function (+, -, ×, ÷) mathematics, while other problems can only be solved extremely inefficiently with classical bits and classical gates, with the traveling salesman problem being a legendary example of such a “hard” problem. If you bring in the additional possibilities associated with a quantum computer, however, you no longer have just classical bits and classical gates, but qubits and fundamentally quantum gates. One of the biggest questions in all of computer science is this: which questions and problems, and under which conditions, will the additional options provided by these qubits and quantum gates result in a major computational speedup, and by how much? That speedup is known as either quantum supremacy or quantum advantage. Which useful problems will experience a quantum advantage, and by how much? That’s one of the main goals of the field of quantum complexity . One of the central open problems in that field, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, has just been solved : by an AI company . Here’s what it does — and doesn’t — mean. Many of the different computational complexity classes of problems are shown. The innermost spaces require the smallest amounts of writeable memory in order to solve them, while the larger spaces require larger amounts of writeable memory in order to solve them. Examples, from innermore to outermore complexity classes, include problems that can be solved in logarithmic time, polynomial time, nondeterministic polynomial time, and exponential time, among others. Credit : Qef/Wikimedia Commons/public domain What you see, above, is a map of what’s known as different complexity classes in computer science. Any computational problem is one where you can identify a problem, write down an algorithm for solving that problem, computationally execute that step-by-step algorithm for the specific input associated with that problem, and get an answer. That answer can be a simple binary (yes/no; true/false) answer, which comes for problems that are decision-type problems. However, computational problems include ones that require a more complex quantitative answer: a function problem, a counting problem, or an optimization problem (such as the traveling salesman problem) are all examples of problems more complex than decision problems. One of the most important complexity classes is known as P . P contains all of the problems that can be solved in polynomial time: generally regarded as “efficiently solvable” problems. If you have a deterministic Turing machine, you can solve a problem of class P using a polynomial amount of computational time. If you’ve ever heard of the famed P versus NP conjecture , it’s a debate over whether problems that are “NP hard,” or which seem to require a nondeterministic amount of polynomial time to solve, could actually ever be solved in polynomial time. It is one of the unclaimed Millennium Prize Problems . The difficulty of factoring semiprimes, or large integers in general, forms the basis of RSA public-key cryptography. If someone has the key, i.e., one of the prime factors, it becomes computationally easy and fast to factor it. However, if you don’t have the key, it’s very computationally expensive, as large-scale fault-tolerant computers that can implement Shor’s algorithm are not yet available. Credit : M. Mosca & S.R. Verschoor, Scientific Reports, 2022 Here’s an example that might help you understand the difference between P and NP: I’m going to give you a number, and we’re going to ask if this number is prime. As a simple example (yes, your computer can do this easily), we’re going to pick a relatively small number: 70,747. Is it prime? If we wanted to write an algorithm to determine whether it was prime, you can imagine: dividing by 2, dividing by 3, dividing by 5, dividing by 7, dividing by 11, dividing by 13, dividing by 17, and so on and so on, until you found a prime number that it was divisible by. Either you’d eventually find one, and so you’d know it wasn’t prime, or you would get to a number that was bigger than the square root of the number without finding one, and that would tell you it was prime. For the number I gave you, 70,747, this algorithm would eventually find that it’s divisible by 263, and that when you divide 70,747 by 263, you find that its other divisor is 269. Finding out if 70,747 is a prime number is an example of an NP problem, but if I give you either 263 or 269, verifying that it’s not prime is easy: an example of a P problem. For much larger numbers — like 80-digit numbers, for example — the verification is easy if you know the counterexample, but demonstrating that an “actually prime” 80-digit number is prime is incredibly computationally difficult. It’s not something that, with today’s computational technology, we can easily or readily do. The way solid-state storage devices work today is by the presence or absence of charged particles across a substrate/gate, which inhibits or allows the flow of current, thereby encoding a 0 or a 1. In principle, we can move from bits to qubits by having, instead of a gate with a permanent charge, a quantum bit that reads out only either a 0 or 1 when measured, but that can exist in a superposition of states while operations are being performed on it. Credit : E. Siegel/Treknology Now that we know what different computational complexity classes are, we can turn to the other aspect to this problem: the difference between classical and quantum computers, and the hope of a “quantum speedup” for certain classes of problems. While classical computers are limited to bits and standard classical operations — operations such as AND, NOT, and OR — quantum computers have inherently quantum versions of both of these in addition to just the classical versions of what’s available. The first major difference is that instead of just bits, which are always in a state that’s a “0” or a “1” with zero exceptions, qubits can also exist in an intermediate state. That intermediate state can be a superposition of “part 0” and “part 1” that isn’t necessarily either 100%/0%, 50%/50%, or 0%/100%, but any value in between them. As long as it sums up to 100% probability at every moment in time, all states are allowed. The amount of “0” and the amount of “1” that it has changes for three reasons: as a result of operations performed on it, as a result of a measurement of the state (which always collapses it to either a “0” or a “1”), or as a result of time-evolution. Of course, since this quantum computer isn’t a perfectly isolated environment, there are also sources of noise and errors from the surrounding particles in the system. Therefore, there are also errors introduced, so that the fidelity of your quantum computer is never perfect. Regardless, the fundamental principle holds: qubits can be a mix of “0” and “1” states combined. On the left, a classical “bit” is illustrated: a two-state system that can have either “0” or “1” as its value. On the right, a quantum two-state system, or qubit, is shown.
